Content:
We can move the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}] up or down by adding or subtracting a number. For example, to obtain the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}-3] we perform the following transformations:

Content:
- Take the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}.]
- Translate the graph down by [MATH: 3] units to get the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}-3.]

Content:
The result is the solid blue curve shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bedad4cd2370b9b330ed753fa14e2992]

Content:
Similarly, we can also move the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}] to the left or to the right by adding or subtracting a number to the variable [MATH: x] under the square root. For instance, to obtain the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x-3},] we perform the following transformations:

Content:
- Take the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}.]
- Translate the graph to the right by [MATH: 3] units to get the graph of [MATH: y=\sqrt{x-3}.]

Content:
The result is the solid blue curve shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6c2261bfdb6fcaba4704c5744dc9a10d]

Content:
Remember:

Content:
- Shifting a function up/down/left/right does not change the shape of a graph.
- If [MATH: a] is a positive number, then a transformation of the type [MATH: y=f(x\pm a)] is counter-intuitive: [MATH: f(x+a)] moves the graph to the left by [MATH: a] units, while [MATH: f(x-a)] moves the graph to the right by [MATH: a] units.
